questions.question: State the four conditions necessary for tropical cyclone formation and explain the role each one plays.
questions.expected_answer: Sea surface temperature of at least 26,5 to 27 degrees Celsius with warm water about 50 m deep — supplies moisture whose condensation releases latent heat, the storm's energy source. A position at least five degrees from the equator — provides enough Coriolis force to set the converging air spinning. Converging surface winds in the trade-wind belt — start the inward and upward flow, often from a cluster of thunderstorms. Weak wind shear aloft — allows the rising storm towers to build vertically without being torn apart.

questions.question: Describe the cross-section of a mature tropical cyclone from the centre outward, matching each part to its weather.
questions.expected_answer: The eye at the centre: sinking air, calm, clear, 20 to 50 km wide, lowest pressure. The eye wall around it: a ring of the tallest cumulonimbus where the inward-spiralling air turns upward — the strongest winds and heaviest rain. Beyond it, spiral rain bands curving outward for hundreds of kilometres, delivering rain in pulses separated by quieter gaps, heavier toward the centre.

questions.question: Using Cyclone Freddy as a case study, explain why the storm intensified, weakened and re-intensified along its track, and where its worst human impacts occurred.
questions.expected_answer: Freddy strengthened over the warm Indian Ocean, weakened over Madagascar and Mozambique when landfall cut off its supply of warm water and latent heat, then re-intensified when it looped back over the warm Mozambique Channel — refuelling on evaporation — before a second landfall near Quelimane. Its worst human impacts were inland in Malawi, where extreme rainfall from the decaying storm caused floods and mudslides on deforested slopes, causing most of the deaths, along with displacement and cholera outbreaks.
